extraction.name: SWE-Gym
extraction.description: SWE-Gym is the first training environment for software engineering agents, containing 2,438 real-world task instances from 11 popular Python repositories. Each instance comprises a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. The environment enables training of language model-based SWE agents and verifiers with executable feedback.
extraction.creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
extraction.rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym comprises 2,438 real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories. Tasks were extracted using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script to convert repositories into task instances, each corresponding to a GitHub issue including the natural language description of the issue, a snapshot of the repository in which the issue was created, and a set of unit tests. Over 358 repositories, 64,689 task instances were initially extracted (SWE-Gym Raw). The collection process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours for environment configuration and validation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data was sourced from GitHub pull requests and issues in Python repositories. Initial repositories were filtered using SEART GitHub search to identify Python repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests and 100 contributors. This resulted in 358 repositories from which 64,689 task instances were extracted.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Version training instances were associated with their respective version numbers and environments were set up version-by-version. Dependencies were manually configured for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to ensure that the gold patch (the human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code. After validation and filtering out failed instances, 2,438 unit-test-validated instances from 11 repositories were obtained. Pre-built Docker images for each instance were created, totaling 6 TB.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Unit tests were expert-written and included in the original repositories. Gold patches (human-submitted code diffs) serve as ground truth solutions. For agent trajectory collection, 491 successful trajectories were sampled from gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 with different temperature settings. Each successful trajectory has roughly 19 turns and approximately 19,000 tokens on average. For verifier training, trajectories were labeled as successful or unsuccessful based on whether they passed the unit tests.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For verifier training, trajectories were labeled as successful if they passed unit tests and unsuccessful otherwise. The verifier was trained to predict success probability. Per-instance capping was introduced to mitigate bias toward easier tasks, limiting the maximum number of selected samples per task. A threshold of 2 was found to achieve a good balance between dataset bias and size.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple trajectories per task instance were collected during training (up to 30 rollouts per task for some experiments). For the main training dataset, 491 successful trajectories were collected across 2,438 instances.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script, SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script, OpenHands remote runtime for parallel execution, SGLang for obtaining log probabilities during verifier inference
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that SWE-Gym, models, and agent trajectories are publicly released to facilitate further research. Pre-built Docker images for each instance are publicly released, totaling 6 TB.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. While current models are primarily research artifacts and not yet production-ready, they can support critical open-source infrastructure and potentially make software development more accessible. As these agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with tasks associated with pandas comprising nearly one-third of the total, whereas tasks related to bokeh represent a mere one percent. Repeated sampling shows that task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, where more samples increase solved instances. This introduces a bias toward easier tasks. Per-instance capping was introduced to mitigate this bias. The dataset focuses exclusively on Python repositories, which may limit generalization to other programming languages.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). Tasks in SWE-Gym are on average harder than those included in SWE-Bench. Codebases in SWE-Gym have relatively fewer files than SWE-Bench but a similar number of total lines of code. Gold patches in SWE-Gym have significantly more lines and files edited compared to SWE-Bench. Models have consistently lower performance on SWE-Gym compared to SWE-Bench. The dataset is limited to 2,438 instances with executable environments, though SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 instances without executable environments.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training: SWE-Gym is designed for training software engineering agents and verifiers. It enables supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning approaches. Testing/Validation: The environment can be used to evaluate agent performance through executable unit tests. The paper demonstrates training agents using OpenHands (general-purpose prompting) and MoatlessTools (specialized workflows) scaffolds. Use cases include: (1) Training policy models through rejection sampling fine-tuning on successful trajectories, (2) Training verifier models for inference-time scaling, (3) Self-improvement through iterative policy optimization, (4) Studying training-time and inference-time scaling behaviors.
